difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent with an 'unless' exception. Correct answer must satisfy both conditions and confirm the exception does not apply. Trap (A) satisfies only the first condition; trap (D) meets both conditions but triggers the exception the principle's consequent defers to.
stimulus: A journalist is obligated to grant a source anonymity if (a) the source could plausibly face retaliation for speaking and (b) the information the source provides cannot be reliably obtained elsewhere, unless the source has knowingly provided false information to the journalist on a prior occasion.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Merrin, a city accountant, risks being fired if her employer learns she spoke with a reporter about questionable expenditures. Because many other accountants in the office have access to the same records, the reporter is obligated to grant her anonymity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Orson, a factory foreman, has documented evidence of unreported chemical spills that regulators have been unable to obtain through official channels. Because Orson would likely be dismissed if identified, and has never misled the reporter before, the reporter is obligated to grant him anonymity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pell, a retired engineer, has volunteered details about long-closed safety investigations. Since Pell faces no professional consequences and the information is widely documented in archives, the reporter may decline to grant anonymity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quill, a shipping clerk, faces likely retaliation for disclosing smuggling operations that the reporter cannot corroborate through other witnesses. However, Quill once fabricated a quotation for the same reporter two years ago. The reporter is nonetheless obligated to grant him anonymity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ravi, a lab technician, could lose his visa if identified, and has always been truthful with the reporter. The reporter grants him anonymity even though the same information has already been reported accurately by a rival newspaper.

explanations.correct: Orson satisfies both antecedent conditions — he faces plausible retaliation (dismissal) and the information is not reliably available elsewhere (regulators could not obtain it). The exception does not apply because he has never misled the reporter. The principle's consequent (obligation to grant anonymity) therefore attaches.
explanations.A: Satisfies only condition (a). The information is available through other accountants with the same records, so condition (b) fails.
explanations.C: Misapplies the principle by treating the antecedent's failure as though it licensed a judgment about what the journalist 'may' do; the principle only states what obligation arises when both conditions hold, not permissions when they fail.
explanations.D: Correctly identifies both conditions but then ignores the exception — Quill's prior fabrication triggers the 'unless' clause, which defeats the obligation. The judgment contradicts the principle.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b) — the information is reliably available elsewhere (already reported by a rival). Granting anonymity is not required by the principle.

difficultyReason: Compound antecedent requiring three matching features. Correct answer aligns each feature to the principle's terms. Trap (B) collapses two features into one; trap (E) misreads the 'proportionate' requirement as any penalty whatsoever.
stimulus: A public official may be sanctioned for accepting a gift from a regulated party only if (a) the gift's value materially exceeds customary hospitality and (b) the official had decision-making authority over a matter affecting the giver at the time the gift was accepted. Any sanction imposed must be proportionate to the value of the gift received.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commissioner Aldin accepted a $3,000 watch from a firm whose zoning application he was then reviewing. He is suspended for six months — a sanction proportionate to the gift's value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inspector Belan accepted a catered lunch from a vendor she had already finished auditing two years earlier. She is suspended for two weeks because the lunch exceeded customary hospitality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Director Ceylan accepted an $8,000 vacation package from a contractor, but she had no authority over any matter concerning the contractor. She is sanctioned because the gift's value was plainly excessive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Auditor Derwin accepted a modest holiday fruit basket from a company he was currently auditing. He is sanctioned because he had decision-making authority at the time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulator Estin accepted a $500 sports ticket from a licensee whose renewal he was reviewing. He is permanently barred from public service on the ground that any gift from a regulated party is intolerable.

explanations.correct: Aldin satisfies both antecedent conditions: a $3,000 watch materially exceeds customary hospitality, and he had decision-making authority over the giver's zoning application at the time. A six-month suspension is described as proportionate to the gift's value, matching the principle's consequent requirement.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). Belan had no current decision-making authority over the vendor; the audit had concluded. The principle does not license a sanction.
explanations.C: Fails condition (b). Without authority over any relevant matter, the principle does not authorize a sanction regardless of the gift's value.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a). A modest fruit basket does not materially exceed customary hospitality; authority alone is not enough.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality requirement. A $500 ticket, even if both antecedent conditions are met, does not justify permanent bar — the sanction is not proportionate.

difficultyReason: Conditional with 'unless' exception for emergencies. Correct answer shows both antecedent conditions satisfied with no exception triggered. Trap (C) confuses the exception for the main rule; trap (D) satisfies only one antecedent condition.
stimulus: A physician should disclose a diagnosis to a patient's immediate family only if (a) the patient has given prior written consent to such disclosure and (b) the disclosure would facilitate care the patient is presently receiving, unless an emergency renders the patient incapable of expressing preferences.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Farrow tells Mr. Halden's daughter about Mr. Halden's diabetes because she asks and seems concerned, even though Mr. Halden has not signed any consent form and is currently alert.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Glent, caring for Ms. Ives who signed a consent form last year, informs Ms. Ives's spouse of her new hypertension diagnosis because the spouse will help administer her daily medication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Henner, treating Mr. Jeran who is conscious and has refused to sign any consent, nonetheless informs his brother of Mr. Jeran's test results, citing the emergency exception because Mr. Jeran looks anxious.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Ionne, whose patient Ms. Kell signed a general consent form, tells Ms. Kell's cousin about a diagnosis unrelated to any current treatment because the cousin is curious about family health history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Lamas declines to share any information with Mr. Morn's family, even though Mr. Morn is unconscious after a stroke and his family needs the diagnosis to coordinate immediate care.

explanations.correct: Ms. Ives has given prior written consent, and the disclosure facilitates care she is presently receiving (her spouse will administer her medication). Both antecedent conditions hold, no exception applies, and the judgment that disclosure is appropriate tracks the principle's consequent.
explanations.A: Fails condition (a). No written consent exists, and the patient is alert, so the exception does not apply either.
explanations.C: Misapplies the exception. The patient is conscious and has refused consent; 'anxious' does not render him incapable of expressing preferences. The judgment treats the exception as a freestanding license.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). The diagnosis is unrelated to care the patient is presently receiving, so disclosure to a curious cousin is not authorized.
explanations.E: Misapplies the exception — the patient is incapable of expressing preferences, the emergency exception is precisely meant to apply, and disclosure would be appropriate under the principle. Declining contradicts the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part conjunctive antecedent; correct answer threads both conditions precisely. Trap (A) inverts the 'in advance' requirement; trap (E) meets one condition but not the other.
stimulus: A research institution is justified in retracting a published study only if (a) the study's central empirical claim has been shown to be incorrect and (b) the error cannot be adequately addressed by publishing a correction in place of retraction.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A journal retracts a study after the authors announce in advance that they might publish revisions in the future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A journal retracts a paper whose central finding about a drug's efficacy has been shown wrong by subsequent trials; because the error pervades the paper's data, methods, and conclusions, a correction would not suffice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A journal retracts a paper whose supplemental appendix contains typographical errors, even though the study's main finding remains well-supported.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A journal declines to retract a paper whose central claim has been conclusively refuted, on the ground that retractions are disfavored as a matter of institutional culture.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A journal retracts a study because its central finding turned out to be wrong, despite the fact that a brief erratum would clearly have corrected the single misreported figure at issue.

explanations.correct: The retraction is justified: the central empirical claim (drug efficacy) is shown to be incorrect, and the pervasive nature of the error means a correction would not adequately address it. Both antecedent conditions hold, and retraction is the matching consequent.
explanations.A: Fails both conditions. There is no showing of incorrectness and no showing that correction would be inadequate; 'announced in advance' is not a factor in the principle.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a). The central finding is well-supported; typographical errors in an appendix do not satisfy the antecedent.
explanations.D: Contradicts the principle's implied permissive force — when both conditions are met, retraction is justified; refusing it on cultural grounds disregards the principle.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b). Because a brief erratum would have corrected the error, retraction is not justified even though condition (a) is met.

difficultyReason: Compound antecedent with an exception for substantial public benefit. Correct answer requires both conditions plus a judgment that weighs the exception. Trap (B) wrongly applies the exception; trap (D) satisfies only the first condition.
stimulus: A government agency should refuse to award a contract to a bidder if (a) the bidder has previously defaulted on a similar public contract and (b) credible alternative bidders are available, unless awarding the contract to the defaulting bidder would produce a substantial public benefit unavailable from any alternative.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transportation authority awards a bridge-maintenance contract to Verdin Ltd., which defaulted on a prior bridge contract, because Verdin's bid is the lowest by a small margin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water district awards a treatment contract to Stellan Co., which defaulted on a similar contract last year, reasoning that Stellan has changed its management and probably will not default again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The housing agency refuses a rehabilitation contract to Polmer Inc., which defaulted on a similar public rehabilitation contract two years ago, because three credible alternative bidders have submitted comparable offers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parks department refuses to award a landscaping contract to Nivan Corp., which has never defaulted on any public contract, on the ground that alternative bidders are available.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defense office awards a specialized radar contract to Oberst GmbH, which defaulted on a similar contract, because Oberst alone possesses a patented technology essential to national air-traffic monitoring that no alternative can replicate.

explanations.correct: Polmer satisfies both antecedent conditions — prior default on a similar contract and credible alternative bidders are available. No substantial public benefit is identified that would trigger the exception, so refusal is exactly what the principle prescribes.
explanations.A: Violates the principle — Verdin meets the antecedent conditions (prior default and, implicitly, other bidders exist since a margin is mentioned), yet the authority awards rather than refuses, with no exception triggered.
explanations.B: Misapplies the exception. Management changes and hope of non-default are not 'substantial public benefit unavailable from any alternative.' The antecedent was met and refusal was required.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — Nivan has never defaulted. The principle supplies no basis for refusal.
explanations.E: Correctly invokes the exception (unique patented technology), so the award is consistent with the principle. However, E describes an exception case — the question is which conforms, and E's judgment is that the agency awards; that is permitted, but C more precisely illustrates conformance because the principle's main operative consequent is 'refuse,' and E depends entirely on the exception clause with some ambiguity about comparable alternatives.

difficultyReason: Conditional principle with two joint conditions and a 'proportionate' qualifier on the consequent. Trap (C) meets both antecedent conditions but selects a disproportionate remedy; trap (A) satisfies only one.
stimulus: An employer is justified in terminating an employee for a single policy violation only if (a) the violation caused substantial harm to the company or its customers and (b) the employee was on notice that the conduct was prohibited; otherwise, any discipline imposed should be proportionate to the harm caused.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhelan fires Truso after Truso's single data-entry error caused a customer to receive a duplicate shipment costing $40; Truso had received no prior training on the data-entry protocol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Umber fires Vail after Vail, who had signed the company's confidentiality policy, leaked a client roster that caused the company to lose its largest account worth millions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Welton fires Xeran after Xeran ignored a posted safety rule, resulting in a minor delay that cost the company roughly $200, even though Xeran had attended the mandatory safety briefing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ylarn issues a written warning to Zemi after Zemi, despite signed training records, leaked proprietary source code that caused the company millions in competitive losses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acrell fires Boden, a new hire on his first day, after Boden posted an offhand social-media comment about the company that caused no measurable harm.

explanations.correct: Vail satisfies both conditions — the leak caused substantial harm (loss of the largest account worth millions), and he had notice of the prohibition (signed the confidentiality policy). Termination is the proportionate response to harm of that magnitude, tracking the principle's consequent.
explanations.A: Fails both conditions: $40 is not substantial harm, and Truso had no notice of the protocol. Termination is not justified.
explanations.C: Violates the proportionality qualifier. The harm ($200 delay) was minor; termination is disproportionate even though both antecedent conditions are met.
explanations.D: Meets both antecedent conditions with substantial harm (millions in competitive losses), so termination would be justified; a written warning is disproportionately lenient, contradicting the principle's proportionality requirement.
explanations.E: Fails both conditions — no measurable harm, and a first-day offhand comment suggests no notice of a specific prohibition. Termination is unjustified.

difficultyReason: Principle with two-part antecedent and an 'unless' exception for urgency. Correct answer satisfies both conditions with no exception; trap (D) inverts the exception by treating it as a separate sufficient condition.
stimulus: A legislator ought to abstain from voting on a measure if (a) the measure would financially benefit a member of the legislator's immediate family and (b) the legislator has not publicly disclosed the relationship, unless the vote cannot be postponed and the legislator's participation is necessary for a quorum.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Senator Arun, whose sister owns stock in a company that would benefit from a tax measure, abstains from the vote even though he publicly disclosed the relationship in advance and a quorum was present without him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Representative Balin, whose brother-in-law owns a firm that would profit from a contracting bill, abstains from the vote; she has never disclosed the relationship publicly and the vote could easily be rescheduled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Councilor Cordel votes on a zoning measure that would benefit his uncle's business, even though he has made no public disclosure and the vote is a routine matter that could be taken next week.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Assemblywoman Dorien, whose son would profit from a highway appropriation, abstains during an emergency session where her vote is needed for a quorum and the measure cannot be postponed, citing the urgency exception.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Delegate Eriss, whose father-in-law benefits from a subsidy bill, votes on the measure after publicly disclosing the relationship; her vote is not needed for a quorum and the bill could have waited a week.

explanations.correct: Balin's brother-in-law is an immediate family member whose firm would financially benefit, she has not disclosed the relationship, and the vote could be postponed (so the exception does not apply). Abstention is the precise consequent the principle demands.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — Arun has publicly disclosed the relationship, so the antecedent is not satisfied. The principle does not require abstention; abstaining is not dictated by the rule.
explanations.C: Contradicts the principle. Both conditions are met (undisclosed relationship, family benefit, postponable vote), but Cordel votes rather than abstaining.
explanations.D: Inverts the exception. The exception is precisely designed for this situation (unpostponable vote + quorum necessity), so Dorien should vote, not abstain. Citing the urgency exception to justify abstention reverses the rule's direction.
explanations.E: Ambiguous on condition (b) — Eriss disclosed, so the antecedent fails. The principle does not mandate abstention here. But voting on a self-benefiting measure when waiting is feasible is not addressed, and the judgment does not clearly conform to the rule's operative consequent.

difficultyReason: Compound sufficient condition with an 'unless' clause. Correct answer meets both predicates; trap (C) satisfies the exception rather than the main conditions; trap (E) meets one predicate but not both.
stimulus: A book reviewer is justified in giving a strongly negative review only if (a) the book fails to achieve the goals the author explicitly sets for it and (b) the reviewer has read the book in its entirety, unless the book is a revised edition whose revisions the reviewer has read alongside the prior published review.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Critic Feris writes a strongly negative review of a novel whose stated aim is to depict a coherent fictional society, arguing that the world-building is incoherent; Feris read only the first third of the book before concluding it was unsalvageable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Critic Glint writes a strongly negative review of a biography whose author announced the goal of establishing the subject's hidden role in founding a political party; Glint, having read the full book, concludes the book provides no evidence of any such role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Critic Hanel writes a strongly negative review of a revised edition, having read only the revisions and not the original edition or any prior review of it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critic Indri writes a strongly negative review of a cookbook whose author promised 'quick weeknight meals'; Indri, having read it cover-to-cover, concedes that the recipes do take only 20 minutes but dislikes the photography.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critic Jorsan writes a strongly negative review of a policy book whose author explicitly aimed to defend a particular reform; Jorsan has read the book cover to cover and finds the reform defense forceful and well-documented.

explanations.correct: Glint satisfies both conditions — the book fails to meet its explicit goal (establishing the subject's hidden role), and Glint has read the entire book. The exception is irrelevant (this is not a revised edition). A strongly negative review is justified.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — Feris read only a third of the book. The principle does not license a strongly negative review on partial reading.
explanations.C: Misapplies the exception — the exception requires both the revisions and the prior published review, and Hanel has not read the prior review. The conditions for the exception are not fully satisfied.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — the book achieves its stated goal (quick weeknight meals); dissatisfaction with photography falls outside the stated aims.
explanations.E: Fails condition (a) — the book accomplishes its stated goal. A strongly negative review is not justified by the principle.

difficultyReason: Compound antecedent with exception for the merchant's own wrongdoing. Correct answer satisfies both conditions and confirms the exception does not apply; trap (A) meets only one condition; trap (E) triggers the exception.
stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund on a returned product if (a) the product failed to perform as advertised within the warranty period and (b) the failure was not caused by the consumer's misuse, unless the merchant can show that the consumer had concealed a defect from the merchant at the time of purchase.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Karan is entitled to a full refund on a blender that stopped working after he used it to crush metal bolts, a use not advertised; the blender was still within its warranty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lerin is entitled to a full refund on a laptop that failed to achieve the battery life advertised on the box; the failure occurred within the one-year warranty, resulted from a manufacturing defect, and Lerin had no defect to conceal at the time of purchase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marsha is not entitled to a full refund on a vacuum cleaner that stopped working because she vacuumed water despite the manual's warnings, even though the failure occurred within warranty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nevers is entitled to a partial refund on a printer that failed to print at the advertised speed within warranty, even though the failure was caused by his own firmware tampering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ollim is entitled to a full refund on a used motorcycle whose engine seized within warranty; at purchase, Ollim had inspected the engine privately and concealed from the dealer that its oil seals were already leaking.

explanations.correct: Lerin satisfies both antecedent conditions — advertised performance failure within warranty, not caused by misuse — and the exception does not apply (no concealed defect at purchase). A full refund is exactly what the principle prescribes.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — crushing metal bolts is misuse of a blender. The principle does not entitle Karan to a refund.
explanations.C: Correctly denies a refund, but the judgment is about what the consumer is not entitled to; while consistent with the principle, it describes an antecedent-failure case rather than conforming to the principle's operative consequent (entitlement).
explanations.D: Confuses the principle's consequent. The principle speaks of a full refund; condition (b) is not met (firmware tampering is misuse), so the principle does not entitle Nevers to any refund under its terms.
explanations.E: Triggers the exception — Ollim concealed a known defect from the dealer at the time of purchase. The merchant's showing defeats entitlement, and a full refund is not required.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent with explicit scope limitation. Correct answer satisfies both conditions precisely within scope; trap (B) satisfies neither; trap (D) meets only the first condition.
stimulus: A public university is justified in restricting an invited speaker's appearance on campus only if (a) the speaker's planned remarks would reasonably be expected to cause imminent disruption to ongoing instruction and (b) less restrictive measures would not adequately prevent that disruption; restrictions are never justified merely because the remarks are unpopular.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pren University bars a speaker from campus solely because a faculty committee finds her previously published arguments offensive; classes elsewhere on campus would not have been disrupted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Querst University permits a speaker to appear at its largest auditorium even though credible reports suggest that her remarks will almost certainly trigger a protest inside adjacent lecture halls, disrupting classes; campus police decline to coordinate any crowd management.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rellen University relocates a planned speech from a classroom building to an off-peak evening time in a separate venue, after credible evidence that daytime remarks would disrupt adjacent classes and after ruling out lighter measures that proved insufficient in similar prior events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sorent University cancels a talk because its provost expects that the speaker's arguments will offend many alumni donors, though no disruption to instruction is anticipated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traven University restricts a speaker's use of amplified sound during a campus speech because the amplification — not the content — would disrupt adjacent classes; however, the university does so without first considering whether a smaller sound system would suffice.

explanations.correct: Rellen's relocation satisfies both antecedent conditions — credible evidence of imminent disruption to instruction, and less restrictive measures have been ruled out after prior failure. The restriction is not based on the remarks' unpopularity, honoring the scope limitation. The judgment matches the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle's explicit scope limitation: the restriction is based solely on offensiveness of prior arguments, not on imminent disruption to instruction.
explanations.B: Fails the principle's consequent direction — where both conditions would justify at least some restriction or coordination, Querst takes no action at all. This tests the opposite misapplication.
explanations.D: Violates the scope limitation and fails condition (a) — cancellation rests on offense to donors, not on disruption to instruction.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b) — the university has not determined whether less restrictive measures (a smaller sound system) would suffice before imposing the restriction.
